content.text:
**Finding submitted: deviation (high severity, restrictive covenants).**

**What I found.** The planner flagged sec-1.4 as the likely location and suspected the rule was absent, but the hosting/services article contains no sole-source language. The real exclusivity sits in Article 6 (paragraph p0037, within sec-5.4): Section 6.1 bars *us* — the Company — from participating in any similar internet project for Deerskin Products or substantially similar products, and gives HDI the exclusive right to the "Deerskin" brand for a direct-to-consumer site.

**Why it's a deviation.** Two problems:
- It runs for "the term of this Agreement," and Section 4.1 (p0024) renews the term automatically each year unless terminated — so the restraint is effectively open-ended.
- There is no performance-based exit, even though HDI has hard obligations on site launch and distribution (Sections 1.6, 1.7). That combination is the rule's walk-away scenario.

**Direction check.** I deliberately left alone the provisions that run in our favour: Section 6.2 (our closeout-merchandise carve-out), Section 6.3 (p0042, HDI restricted for two years post-term), and Section 5.2's "exclusive artistic and editorial control," which benefits us. The trademark licence in Section 6.1's second paragraph is already non-exclusive.

**Position taken — fallback, not preferred.** Preferred would be deleting the obligation outright, but that looked disproportionate here: HDI bears all Site design, hosting and promotion costs and gives a reciprocal two-year covenant, so Section 6.1 is part of a genuine mutual bargain. The product scope is also already confined to a defined category. My two-part edit therefore (i) caps the restraint at twelve months from the Effective Date, defining an "Exclusivity Period," and (ii) makes it terminate automatically if HDI misses any service level, availability or delivery date requirement, citing Sections 1.6 and 1.7.

Redline validated `ok:true` before submission. One caveat worth your judgement: I anchored the exit to "service level, availability or delivery date requirements" generically because the agreement has no dedicated SLA section — if you want a tighter trigger, Sections 1.6 and 1.7 could be made the exclusive hooks.
